1.pericope_label: El Shaddai appears after thirteen years' silence: walk before me, and be thou perfect

schools.summary: Gill counts the interval: the ninety-ninth year falls thirteen years after Ishmael's birth, and the age is noted so that the power of God might be the more manifest. Calvin makes more of the silence, holding that Moses passes over those years not because nothing worthy of remembrance occurred but because the Spirit of God selects what is most necessary to be known, and that the length of the interval teaches us how long Abram remained satisfied with the son who should at length be rejected, deluded by a fallacious appearance. The want of offspring had stirred him to constant prayers and sighings; but now, falsely supposing he had obtained his wish, he was led away by the presence of a son after the flesh from the expectation of a spiritual seed. So the goodness of God shows itself in raising him beyond his own expectation, since he suddenly hears that what it never came into his mind to ask is granted him — had he been daily offering importunate prayers for this blessing, we should not so plainly have seen that it was conferred by free gift.

Henry gives three reasons why the promise was so long deferred: to correct Abram's over-hasty marrying of Hagar, since comforts we sinfully anticipate are justly delayed; that with Abram and Sarai so far stricken in age God's power might be the more magnified and their faith the more tried; and that a child so long waited for might be an Isaac, a son indeed. He notes too that God's extraordinary appearances were intermitted all that while, so that Abram's communion with him ran in the usual ways of ordinances and providences — there being special comforts which are not the daily bread even of the best saints, who on this side heaven have convenient food but not a continual feast.

Clarke derives the title from a root meaning to pour out — I am that God who pours out blessings, who gives them richly, abundantly, continually — and on the command that follows he will not let sincerity soften into an excuse. Some say the words mean only be sincere, since perfect obedience is impossible; if by sincerity they mean good desires with an impure heart and a spotted life, no such thing is implied in the text or in the original word, though if sincerity be taken in its proper and literal sense he has no objection, since sincere is compounded of sine cera, without wax, a metaphor from clarified honey out of which every atom of the comb is separated. Wesley draws the consequence: upright walking with God is the condition of our interest in his all-sufficiency, for if we neglect him or dissemble with him we forfeit the benefit of our relation to him.

Ellicott takes El Shaddai for an archaic title meaning strong so as to overpower, and notes its range: besides its use in Genesis it is employed by Balaam, by Naomi, and in the book of Job, where it occurs thirty-one times, so that it may be regarded as one of the more general worldwide titles of the Most High. He sets beside it the statement in Exodus, made with evident reference to this place, that El Shaddai was the name revealed to the patriarchs and that God was not known to them by his name Jehovah; yet here, in a passage the commentators call Elohistic, Jehovah appears to Abram and says, I am El Shaddai, the gist of the passage being the identification of the two.

debates.question: What does the command to be perfect require?

positions.position: not the mere sincerity that excuses an impure heart, but sincerity in its literal sense — sine cera, without wax, as honey clarified of every atom of the comb
upright walking as the condition of any interest in the all-sufficiency just named

themes: the Lord appeared to Abram and said, I am the Almighty God
walk before me, and be thou perfect
thirteen years between Ishmael and the promise

2.pericope_label: The covenant given rather than cut, and Abram on his face before God

schools.summary: Calvin distinguishes the two parts of what was promised: the first a declaration of gratuitous love with the promise of a happy life annexed, the second an exhortation to the sincere endeavour to cultivate uprightness. God had given in a single word only a slight taste of his grace before descending at once to the design of his calling, and now subjoins a fuller declaration so that Abram may the more willingly form his mind and life to reverence — as if he had said, see how kindly I indulge thee, for I do not require integrity simply on the ground of my authority, which I might justly do, but, whereas I owe thee nothing, I condescend graciously to engage in a mutual covenant. Nor does Calvin allow that anything new is said, since God recalls the covenant made before and now confirms its certainty, not being wont to utter new oracles which might destroy the credit or obscure the light of those which preceded. He reads the silence of the prostration as the confession itself: Abram testifies that he acknowledges God, in whose presence all flesh ought to keep silence, and that he reverently receives whatever God is about to speak, declaring more fully by his silence than if he had spoken with a loud and sounding voice that he yields obedience to the word. Gill guards the posture against a rabbinic explanation: it was not because Abram was as yet uncircumcised, as the Targum of Jonathan has it, other Jewish writers observing that before circumcision he fell when God spoke but afterwards sat and stood, for not only uncircumcised persons such as Balaam but circumcised ones such as Ezekiel and Joshua have fallen on their faces at a divine appearance.

Clarke describes the eastern manner of the prostration: the person went down upon his knees, lowered his head to them and touched the earth with his forehead — a very painful posture, but significative of great humiliation and reverence. Wesley offers two constructions of the act, that Abram fell either as one overcome by the brightness of the divine glory, as Daniel and John did likewise, or as one ashamed of himself and blushing to think of the honours done to one so unworthy; he looks upon himself with humility and upon God with reverence, and in token of both falls on his face.

Ellicott marks a change in the verb: in the earlier account of the covenant the Hebrew word for making it is cut, referring to the severing of the victims, whereas here it is give or place, and implies an act of grace on God's part. He reckons the waiting too — twenty-five years since Ur of the Chaldees and fourteen or fifteen since the ratification — and finds the time at length arrived for the fulfilment, in token of which Abram and Sarai were to change their names and all the males to be brought near to God by a solemn sacrament. Keil sets out what the covenant contained on God's side under three heads: that he would make Abram the father of a multitude of nations, the ancestor of nations and of kings; that he would be God to him and to his posterity through all their generations, in an eternal covenant relation; and that he would give them for an everlasting possession the land in which he had wandered as a foreigner.

debates.question: Why did Abram fall on his face?

positions.position: overcome by the brightness of the divine glory, or ashamed at the honours done to one so unworthy
in token of adoration, the silence itself being the confession that he receives whatever God will speak
not, as the Targum of Jonathan supposes, because he was as yet uncircumcised

Abram fell on his face, and God talked with him

4.pericope_label: A father of many nations, and the new name whose etymology no one can fix

schools.summary: Calvin fastens on the emphatic pronoun with which God opens. God declares that he is the speaker, in order that absolute authority may appear in his words; for since our faith can rest on no other foundation than his eternal veracity, we must be informed that what is proposed to us has proceeded from his sacred mouth. Although all angels and men should speak to us, never would their authority appear sufficiently great to confirm our minds, and we cannot but waver until that voice sounds from heaven, I am; if myriads of men set themselves in opposition and proudly exclaim, We, we, let this single word of God suffice to dissipate the empty sound of multitudes. On the multitude of nations he argues that the promise reaches further than descent: different nations did spring from the patriarch, but Moses looked beyond that, because the Gentiles were to be by faith inserted into the stock of Abram though not descended from him after the flesh. Abraham was therefore called father of many nations not because his seed was to be divided into many nations, but because many nations were to be gathered together unto him. Gill takes the promise of fruitfulness literally: not only a son by Sarai from whom sprang a numerous offspring, but six sons by Keturah, heads of large nations.

Henry notes the solemnity with which the promise is introduced — as for me, says the great God, behold and admire it, my covenant is with thee — a covenant of God's own making, in which he glories, and so may we. He takes the promise that Abram shall be father of many nations in two senses. His seed after the flesh should be very numerous, in Isaac and Ishmael as well as the sons of Keturah, and there have probably been more of the children of men descended from Abraham than from any one man at an equal distance from Noah; and all believers in every age should be looked upon as his spiritual seed, so that he is called not only the friend of God but the father of the faithful.

Wesley puts the second sense in the rabbinic phrase: father of those, in every nation, who by faith enter into covenant with God and are gathered under the wings of the divine Majesty. Clarke finds the etymology of the new name very difficult and reviews the attempts. Some suppose it a contraction for a phrase meaning the father of a great multitude; Rabbi Solomon Jarchi defines it cabalistically and says that its numeral letters amount to two hundred and forty-eight, the exact number of the bones in the human body, so that before the added letter it was five short of that perfection. Then one more: William Alabaster most wisely says that the first form of the name signifies father of the Romans, and consequently the pope, so that Abraham was pope the first — which, Clarke observes, is just as likely as some of the preceding etymologies. From all these learned as well as puerile conjectures we may see the difficulty of ascertaining the true meaning, though the concordance makers and proper-name explainers find no difficulty at all, and pronounce as readily as if they had been in the divine council when the name was imposed.

Ellicott protests that of many nations is a feeble rendering, since the word literally signifies a confused noise like the din of a populous city — Abram is to be father of a thronging crowd of nations. Keil states what was required on the other side: Abraham and his descendants in all generations were to keep the covenant, circumcising every male in the house as its sign.

debates.question: In what sense is Abraham father of many nations?

positions.position: in both senses at once — a numerous seed after the flesh, and all believers in every age as his spiritual seed
not because his seed was to be divided into many nations, but because many nations were to be gathered together unto him by faith
literally, in the sons by Sarai and the six by Keturah who became heads of large nations

themes: thy name shall be Abraham, for a father of many nations have I made thee
I will make thee exceeding fruitful, and kings shall come out of thee
the etymology of the new name

7.pericope_label: The everlasting covenant, and the token that binds both parties to it

schools.summary: Gill takes establish strictly: God does not merely renew the covenant, but confirms it by the token that follows. Calvin insists the seed here meant is the natural one, and that those are deceived who think only the elect are pointed out, or the faithful of every people indiscriminately comprehended. Paul teaches of Abraham's natural descendants that they are holy branches proceeded from a holy root; and lest anyone restrict that to the shadows of the law or evade it by allegory, he elsewhere says that Christ came to be a minister of the circumcision. If it be objected that this will not agree with reckoning as Abraham's children those by faith ingrafted into his body, Calvin reconciles the two by distinct degrees of adoption. Before it the condition of the whole world was one and the same; but as soon as it was said, I will be a God to thee and to thy seed after thee, the Church was separated from the nations, as in the creation the light emerged out of the darkness. Then Israel was received as the flock of God into their own fold, while the other nations wandered like wild beasts through mountains, woods and deserts. So a twofold class of sons presents itself: since the whole body of the people is gathered into the fold by one voice, all are in that respect accounted children; but in the innermost sanctuary none are reckoned sons save those in whom the calling is inwardly sealed by the Spirit.

Henry finds the covenant's continuance intimated in three things. It is established, not to be altered or revoked, but as firm as divine power and truth can make it; it is entailed, a covenant not with Abraham only, for then it would die with him, but with his seed after him, not his seed after the flesh only but his spiritual seed; and it is everlasting in the evangelical sense, from everlasting in the counsels of it and to everlasting in the consequences of it, its external administration transmitted with the seal to the seed of believers, its internal by the Spirit to Christ's seed in every age. He turns then to the token, for the sake of which the covenant is itself called the covenant of circumcision. It is a sign and a seal, at once a confirmation of the promises which were God's part and an obligation to the duty which was theirs, for circumcision made men debtors to do the whole law; those who will have God to be theirs must resolve to be to him a people. It was a bloody ordinance, since all things by the law were purged with blood; but Christ's blood being shed, such ordinances are abolished, and circumcision gives way to baptism. It was peculiar to the males, though the women were included too — in our kingdom, Henry remarks, the oath of allegiance is required only from men.

Wesley dwells on the first promise. All the privileges of the covenant, all its joys and all its hopes, are summed up in the words that God would be their God, and a man needs desire no more to make him happy; for what God is himself, that he will be to his people — wisdom to guide and counsel them, power to protect and support them, goodness to supply and comfort them. This is enough, Wesley adds, yet not all. Clarke takes the everlasting of the promise in its own proper meaning, as the following words prove: to be a God unto thee and thy seed after thee. As the soul is to endure for ever, it shall eternally stand in need of the supporting power and energy of God; and as the gospel dispensation shall reign as long as sun and moon endure, its consequences eternal, so must the covenant be on which these are founded.

debates.question: Who is the seed with whom the covenant is established?

positions.position: the natural descendants by lineal descent, with a further and inward degree of adoption for those in whom the calling is sealed by the Spirit
not his seed after the flesh only but his spiritual seed, the covenant being everlasting in the evangelical sense

themes: I will establish my covenant for an everlasting covenant
to be a God unto thee, and to thy seed after thee
the token that obliges both parties

8.pericope_label: Canaan for an everlasting possession, and whether the rite came out of Egypt

schools.summary: Gill distinguishes the two ways the land is given: to Abraham in right, to his seed in possession and inheritance; and he adds that circumcision is called the covenant only improperly, the promise itself having been given before, so that it is but the sign. Calvin sets the rite among the ancient ways of recording a compact. Covenants were committed to public records, engraven in brass, sculptured on stones, that their memory might be the more celebrated; so here God inscribes his covenant in the flesh of Abraham, a solemn memorial of the adoption by which his family had been elected God's peculiar people. Since Moses calls circumcision the covenant of God, the promise of grace was included in it; had it been only a mark of external profession, the name of covenant would be by no means suitable, for a covenant is not otherwise confirmed than as faith answers to it. A sacrament is nothing else than a visible word, an image of that grace which the word more fully illustrates; and as soon as the sign meets our eyes the word ought to sound in our ears. So when Abraham is commanded to keep the covenant, God does not enjoin the bare ceremony but designs that he should regard the end; for the promise is the very soul of the sign, and whenever it is torn away nothing remains but a lifeless and vain phantom. On the restriction to one sex Calvin notes that the promise was made alike to both, and females as well as males had need of confirmation; the covenant was graven on the bodies of the males with this condition annexed, that the females also, as their associates, should partake of the sign.

Clarke thinks the everlasting of the possession bears its accommodated meaning, signifying the completion of the divine counsel in a particular dispensation; and it is literally true that Israel held Canaan until the Mosaic dispensation terminated in the full introduction of the gospel. Yet since the spiritual and temporal covenants are blended, the former typified by the latter, the word may even here be taken as ever-during, because the spiritual blessings it signified shall have no end — and hence it is immediately added, I will be their God, not for a time but for ever. On the origin of the rite he goes at the chronology: Herodotus reports that the Colchians, Egyptians and Ethiopians alone have used circumcision from the remotest period, and that the Syrians of Palestine acknowledge they had it from the Egyptians; but Herodotus flourished only four hundred and eighty-four years before the Christian era, while Jacob went down into Egypt more than eighteen hundred years before Christ, so the presumption runs the other way. Wesley reads the grant as Clarke does: Canaan had been promised before, but here for an everlasting possession, as a type of that everlasting rest which remains for the people of God; this is that better country to which Abraham had an eye, and had God not designed it he would have been ashamed to be called their God.

Ellicott calls the statement of Herodotus very loose and too far posterior to Abram's time for implicit confidence, and observes that the monuments and the mummies show the rite becoming general in Egypt only in quite recent times. He then sets the question aside as merely archaeological, since the rite was just as appropriate a sign if borrowed from institutions already existing as if then first used. Its fitness lay in representing a new birth, the putting off of the old man and dedication of the new unto holiness — the flesh cast away that the spirit might grow strong; and the change of name in Abram and Sarai was typical of that change of condition, for they had been born again, and so must again be named.

debates.question: Did Israel take circumcision from the Egyptians?

positions.position: no — Herodotus wrote fourteen centuries after Jacob went down into Egypt, so the presumption runs the other way
the monuments and mummies show the rite general in Egypt only recently, and in any case the question is merely archaeological, since a borrowed sign would serve as well

every man child among you shall be circumcised
whether the rite was learned from Egypt

11.pericope_label: The token in the flesh, the eighth day, and the reach of the command over the household

schools.summary: Gill reports the practice from the Jewish writers. A dish of sand received the foreskin, which Buxtorf explains as a token that their seed should be as the sand of the sea, and with respect to the old serpent that deceived man, whose food is the dust of the earth. The canons allow circumcising with anything that cuts, a flint or glass, excepting cane or reed because of the danger; but iron is best, and all Israelites use a knife. Calvin admits the command looks strange and unaccountable at first sight, since the subject is the sacred covenant, in which righteousness, salvation and happiness are promised, and who can say it is reasonable that the sign of so great a mystery should consist in this? But as Abraham had to become a fool in order to prove himself obedient, so whoever is wise will soberly and reverently receive what God seems to us foolishly to have commanded. Yet an analogy may be sought, since signs appointed to assist our infirmity should be accommodated to our capacity or they would be unprofitable. Calvin finds two reasons for it. The first is to show that whatever is born of man is polluted, whatever men have by generation being condemned in this appointment, that the corruption of nature being manifest they might mortify their flesh; whence circumcision was a sign of repentance. The second is that salvation should proceed from the blessed seed: if the token of so singular a favour seems absurd in that part of the body, let him become ashamed of his own salvation, which flowed from the loins of Abraham; God has thus confounded the wisdom of the world, the more completely to abase the pride of the flesh. On the eighth day Calvin canvasses the explanations and refuses to choose. Some say God spared the children for their tenderness, since it was not without danger to wound the newly born; others seek a mystery in the number, the seven days signifying the present life and the eighth a new one, while others referred it to the resurrection of Christ. Calvin thinks the seven probable and consonant with reason, but because such a reason is never given in Scripture he dare affirm nothing. What is certain is that God in this symbol has so represented the destruction of the old man as yet to show that he restores men to life. He notes too the reach of the command over the household: slaves were formerly scarce reckoned among men, but God out of regard to his servant adopts them as his own sons, gathering freemen and slaves without respect of persons; every family of the pious ought to be a church.

Clarke takes the token as a sign of spiritual things, circumcision in the flesh signifying the purification of the heart from all unrighteousness, as God showed in the law itself. That some of the Jews had a just notion of its spiritual intention he proves from the book Zohar, quoted by Ainsworth: at what time a man is sealed with this holy seal, thenceforth he seeth the holy blessed God properly, and the holy soul is united to him; but if he keep not this sign, by the breath of God they perish, because this seal was not kept. On the eighth day he observes that before it they were unclean, and that neither calf nor lamb nor kid was offered to God until it was eight days old, for the same reason, circumcision being a consecration of the person to God.

Ellicott adds that this is just one week after birth, the day of birth counted among the eight. On the extension of the rite to the whole house he presses the order of it: the bought slave was circumcised first and instructed afterwards, no profession of faith required, admitted in right of his master.

positions.position: because before it the child was reckoned unclean, as no calf or lamb or kid was offered until eight days old
possibly for the child’s tenderness, possibly because seven signifies the present life and the eighth a new one — but Scripture never gives the reason, so nothing may be affirmed

14.pericope_label: Cutting off, and the change of Sarai's name

schools.summary: Gill traces the chain the canons lay down: the commandment lies upon a father to circumcise his son and upon a master his servants; if a father does not, the sanhedrim are bound to; and if they do not, the man when grown must circumcise himself, and if he does not he is guilty of cutting off. Calvin reads the threat as a measure of God's care. Since he benignantly offers a pledge of his love and of eternal life, for what purpose does he add threatening but to rouse the sluggishness of those who should run with diligence? The denunciation virtually charges men with foul ingratitude, in rejecting or despising the grace of God. Since God threatens only despisers, the uncircumcision of children would do them no harm if they died before the eighth day, for the bare promise was effectual to their salvation; God did not so attest it by external signs as to restrict his own working to them, and the covenant is not violated when the power of keeping it has been taken away. Nor is any fault of their own charged on infants: as God adopts the son in the person of his father, so when the father repudiates the benefit the infant is said to cut himself off from the Church. Calvin carries the argument over to baptism: whoever, having neglected it, feigns himself contented with the bare promise tramples as much as in him lies upon the blood of Christ; but to consign to destruction infants whom a sudden death has not allowed to be presented is a cruelty originating in superstition. On the change of name Gill marks the sequence, God speaking of Sarai only after changing Abraham's name and giving the covenant of circumcision; and Calvin recalls how the promise had been anticipated, Sarai having been too precipitate in substituting her handmaid without any command from God, and Abraham too pliant in following his wife, yet their fault did not prevent God from giving them the seed from whose expectation they had in a manner cut themselves off, and his gratuitous kindness shines the clearer for coming to men who impede its course by obstacles of their own. On the name Calvin notes that the letter dropped has among the Hebrews the force of the possessive pronoun, so that God designs her to be celebrated everywhere and without exception as a sovereign and princess.

Henry adds that God reveals the purposes of his good will by degrees, having told Abraham long before that he should have a son but never till now that he should have one by Sarai; and he hears in the new name that from her should come the Messiah the prince, the prince of the kings of the earth.

Clarke rejects the notion of a sudden temporal death: the meaning seems to be that such should have no right to nor share in the blessings of the covenant, temporal and spiritual alike; and if so, eternal death was implied, since one unpurified could not enter into glory. Wesley puts the contrast in the name plainly: Sarai signifies my princess, as if her honour were confined to one family; Sarah, a princess of multitudes.

Ellicott sets two readings of the penalty against each other. Jewish commentators leave the offender to the direct interposition of God, who would punish him with childlessness and premature death; most Christian commentators suppose he was put to death by the magistrate, which Ellicott holds untenable, since a constant distinction is drawn between the penalty of death and being cut off: blasphemy and murder are punished with death, the eating of blood otherwise. The punishment seems rather excommunication or outlawry: he forfeited his privileges as a member of the nation, could claim no protection from the elders for life and property, and could not take his place at the gate of the city. On the name he makes Sarai probably princely, an adjective of the same form as shaddai.

debates.question: What is meant by being cut off from his people?

positions.position: no sudden temporal death, but exclusion from the blessings of the covenant, and so eternal death implied
not death at the magistrate’s hand but excommunication or outlawry — loss of protection and of a place at the gate of the city
said of the infant only in the person of the father who repudiated the benefit, since God threatens despisers and not those from whom the power of keeping was taken away

thou shalt not call her name Sarai, but Sarah shall her name be

16.pericope_label: Sarah blessed, Abraham's laughter, and the prayer for Ishmael

schools.summary: Gill divides the blessing three ways with the Targum of Jonathan, which adds in her body: fruitfulness where she had been barren, spiritual blessings in her soul, and in both eternal life. On the laughter he says only that Abraham fell on his face in reverence of the divine Being, as amazed at what was told him. Calvin refuses the reading that makes it pure joy. He does not assent to those who suppose the laughter flowed solely from joy, but thinks Abraham as one astonished, partly exulting and partly carried beyond himself in admiration; the novelty so strikes him that for a short time he is confounded, yet prostrate on the earth he by faith adores the power of God. The admiration did not obstruct the course of God's power and was not contrary to faith; rather the strength of faith shone the more brightly in surmounting an obstacle so arduous. On the prayer that follows Calvin hears a mind still perturbed: as if he did not dare hope for all that God promises, Abraham fixes on the son already born, not rejecting the promise of fresh offspring but contented with the favour received, provided God's liberality should not extend further; and to live before the Lord is to be preserved in safety under his protection. Gill accounts for the prayer from Ishmael's standing in the house, since he was grown and had doubtless a large share in his father's affections, and it is highly probable he had begun to think him the promised seed, having so long no other son and Sarah past bearing.

Clarke ranks Sarah highest of all: she stands at the head of all the women of the Old Testament for her extraordinary privileges, and he is quite of Calmet's opinion that she was a type of the blessed Virgin; Paul makes her a type of the heavenly Jerusalem, and as all true believers are children of Abraham, so all faithful holy women are daughters of Sarah. On the laughter he will have nothing but joy in it, and is astonished to find learned and pious men taking it for weakness of faith when they have the most positive assurance from the Spirit himself that Abraham staggered not at the promise but gave glory to God; from this very circumstance Isaac had his name, for the word we change into Isaac signifies laughter. He takes the petition for Ishmael as asking that he might head a prosperous and potent people. Wesley keeps it a laughter of delight, not of distrust: Abraham rejoiced to see Christ's day, for as he saw heaven in the promise of Canaan, so he saw Christ in the promise of Isaac. On the prayer he draws the lesson that the great thing we should desire of God for our children is that they may live before him, kept in covenant and having grace to walk in their uprightness.

Ellicott marks the verse a turning point: this is the first place where it was definitely promised that Abram's heir should be Sarah's own son, and that must be remembered in estimating their conduct in the matter of Hagar, for they had long waited and hoped before taking measures of their own; the rest he would render, she shall become nations, kings of peoples shall spring from her. On the laughter he doubts the neat Jewish division of Abraham's from Sarah's, and grants that belief was mixed with surprise: one ready to sacrifice his only son would not be staggered by strangeness, yet the thought of Sarah bearing at ninety might easily present itself in a ludicrous aspect. What the double laughter brings out is that Isaac's birth was contrary to nature. He presses the cost of the change for Ishmael, who for thirteen years had been the son of the house and probably regarded as the true heir, so that mingled with Abraham's joy was the pain, natural to a father, of knowing that the transference of the promise meant the deposition of one who had so long held the post of honour; stoicism would have repressed that upright and natural feeling, but God hears and accepts the father's prayer.

positions.position: joy only, and nothing else — the Spirit himself testifies that he staggered not at the promise
not joy alone but astonishment; the novelty so struck him that for a moment he was confounded, and faith shone the brighter for surmounting it
joy uppermost, yet mixed with a surprise in which the thing promised could present itself in a ludicrous aspect

themes: I will bless her, and she shall be a mother of nations
Abraham fell upon his face, and laughed
O that Ishmael might live before thee

19.pericope_label: Isaac named, Ishmael blessed with earthly things, and God goes up from Abraham

schools.summary: Gill takes the repetition as deliberate: it is said again to remove any doubt in Abraham's mind, and to show that the promise of a son by Sarah was not superseded by his prayer for Ishmael, for whom he might well have a greater flow of natural affection. Calvin hears God rousing a slumbering mind, as if he had said: the sight of one favour prevents thee from raising thyself higher, and thou dost confine thy thoughts within too narrow limits; enlarge thy mind now to receive also what I promise concerning Sarah, for the door of hope ought to be open enough to admit the word in its full magnitude. Since Abraham had framed a false hope not founded on the word of God, it had first to be dislodged, that he might fix the anchor of his faith on the firm truth of God. Calvin will not let the distinction between the brothers become an exclusion: it might seem absurd that God should command Ishmael, whom he deprives of his grace, to be circumcised, but though the Lord constitutes Isaac the head from whom the covenant of salvation is to flow, he does not entirely exclude Ishmael, joining him to his brother as an inferior member until he cut himself off from his father's house. The next promise discriminates the two sons more clearly. In promising Ishmael wealth, dignity and other things of the present life, God proves him a son according to the flesh; the covenant with Isaac rises above the world and this frail life. God promises him liberally and profusely whatever is desirable in this earthly life, yet accounts as nothing all those gifts in comparison with that covenant; whence neither wealth nor power nor any temporal gift is promised to the sons of the Spirit, but an eternal blessing possessed in this world only by hope. On the departure Calvin holds that the ascent shows Abraham certainly knew the vision was from God, and the pious must be assured of that, lest they be carried hither and thither; God does not now openly ascend before our eyes, but his majesty is not less resplendent in this, that he raises us upwards by transforming us into his image. Gill closes with a limit: the highest enjoyments of God here are not lasting, for uninterrupted communion with him is reserved for another world.

Clarke follows the twelve princes into history. From Ishmael proceeded the tribes of the Arabs, anciently and still a numerous and powerful people; and quotes Bishop Newton that human sagacity could not have foreseen that a man's whole posterity should so nearly resemble him, retaining the same inclinations, habits and customs through all ages. These are the only people besides the Jews who have subsisted distinct from the beginning, and they resemble each other: both descend from Abraham and boast of it, both are circumcised and derive the rite from him, and both had originally twelve patriarchs for princes. We may the more confidently believe what is related of Abraham and Ishmael when we see it verified in their posterity at this day. On the departure Clarke observes that God ascended evidently before Abraham, proof enough that no human being, no earthly angel, had talked with him; and asks whether it was not in nearly the same way that Christ ascended before his disciples. Wesley is gentler with Ishmael: we may charitably hope that spiritual blessings too were bestowed on him, though the visible church was not brought out of his loins.

Ellicott finds the same force in the word order: in the Hebrew the word rendered indeed comes first, meant to remove all doubt or desire for any other turn of affairs, and it should read, for a certainty Sarah thy wife shall bear thee a son. The name is a perpetual memorial that Isaac's birth was naturally such an impossibility as to excite ridicule.

23.pericope_label: The selfsame day: Abraham circumcises his whole house

schools.summary: Calvin weighs the cost. Abraham must have been entirely devoted to God, since he did not hesitate to inflict on himself a wound attended with acute pain and not without danger of life, nor defer the work to another day. Nor was he without perplexing thoughts: why has he put me off to extreme old age, who have been so long harassed with adverse affairs and yet never swerved from the word of God? and what does this mean, that I cannot be saved unless I, with one foot almost in the grave, thus mutilate myself? Two further things Calvin observes. The first is the difficulty of the work, for Abraham had in his house a multitude nearly equal to a people, and it was scarcely credible that so many would suffer themselves to be wounded and apparently made a laughingstock; it was justly to be feared that the greater part would rise up against him; yet relying on the word of God he attempts what seemed impossible. The second is how faithfully his family had been instructed, since not only home-born slaves but foreigners and men bought with money meekly received a wound troublesome and shameful to carnal sense; holding them under holy discipline, he had the reward of his diligence in finding them tractable in so arduous an affair. Gill notices the order. Abraham took his son first, to set an example to his servants, that they might the more readily comply when they saw his only son circumcised before their eyes; and the men of the house were circumcised by their own will, not forced, as Aben Ezra rightly observes, having been trained up before in religion. His age is noted for the same reason: he did not object that he could not bear the pain, or that it were shameful for a man of his years to be uncovered before his servants. From Jarchi he takes the point that it was done in the day and not the night, which shows he feared neither the heathen nor mockers, and that the men of that generation might not say, if we had seen him we would not have suffered it.

Henry takes the obedience apart. It was implicit: he did as God had said and did not ask why or wherefore, God's will being to him not only a law but a reason. It was speedy, in the selfsame day; sincere obedience is never dilatory, and while the command is yet sounding in our ears it is good to apply ourselves to it at once, lest we put it off to a more convenient season. It was universal: he did not circumcise his family and excuse himself, but set them an example, nor took the comfort of the seal to himself only — a pattern, Henry says, for masters of families, since they and their houses must serve the Lord. And it was done though much might be objected. Circumcision was painful, and to grown men shameful; while they were sore and unfit for action their enemies might take advantage, as Simeon and Levi did against the Shechemites; and Abraham was ninety-nine, and had been justified long since. Yet God's command sufficed to answer these and a thousand such objections.

Clarke rests on the consent of the household. Had not Abraham, and his son who was of age to judge for himself, and all the family been fully convinced that this was of God, they could not have submitted to it; a rite so painful, so repugnant to every feeling of delicacy, could never have sprung from the imagination of man. Nor could it have been designed as a distinction from other people, since it was a sign never to appear: the individual alone knew that he bore it in his flesh.
Ellicott notes that from Ishmael's age the Mohammedans defer circumcision to the thirteenth year.
